issues.legal_issue: Continuing a criminal prosecution arising from a civil dispute that has been finally adjudicated constitutes an abuse of the process of the court when the prosecution is manipulated to harass the accused and restrict personal liberty.
material_facts: The dispute arose from a joint venture agreement and allegations concerning investments, funding commitments, and company assets; the Company Law Board adjudicated the parties’ dispute, and the High Court affirmed its directions.

After an earlier complaint about the same dispute was dismissed, the complainant filed another complaint without disclosing that dismissal; the resulting criminal case was later closed, then reopened for further investigation and led to a charge-sheet.
The criminal proceedings led to warrants and restrictions affecting the accused persons’ ability to travel, and the Court found that the process had been manipulated and misused to harass them.
issues.conclusion: The criminal proceedings arising from the registered case should be quashed because their continuation would be an abuse of the process of the court and contrary to the ends of justice.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a High Court may quash criminal proceedings to prevent abuse of process or secure the ends of justice; its power under Article 226 may also be used where police investigation powers are exercised mala fide. Proceedings may be stayed or quashed where trying the accused would be unfair or the process has been misused, including where criminal prosecution is used to pressure parties in a civil dispute or to wreak private vengeance. The Court relied on Connelly v. Director of Public Prosecutions, Hui Chi-Ming v. The Queen, Bennett v. Horseferry Road Magistrates’ Court, R. v. Derby Crown Court ex p Brooks, R. v. Beckford, State of Karnataka v. L. Muniswamy, State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, Zandu Pharmaceutical Works Ltd. v. Mohd. Sharaful Haque, Indian Oil Corpn. v. NEPC India Ltd., Inder Mohan Goswami v. State of Uttaranchal, G. Sagar Suri v. State of U.P., S.N. Sharma v. Bipen Kumar Tiwari, State of West Bengal v. Swapan Kumar Guha, and Uma Shankar Gopalika v. State of Bihar. The Court also noted Article 21’s protection of personal liberty.

rule.if: criminal_prosecution_challenged and underlying_dispute_civil_and_finally_resolved and repeated_complaints_over_same_dispute and earlier_dismissal_not_disclosed and process_used_to_harass_or_pressure and accused_liberty_restricted

predicates.criminal_prosecution_challenged: The accused challenged the continuation of a criminal prosecution arising from a complaint or registered case.
predicates.underlying_dispute_civil_and_finally_res: The underlying dispute concerned civil or commercial dealings and had been finally adjudicated by a competent forum.
predicates.repeated_complaints_over_same_dispute: The complainant initiated repeated criminal complaints concerning the same underlying dispute.
predicates.earlier_dismissal_not_disclosed: When pursuing a later complaint, the complainant did not disclose that an earlier complaint about the same dispute had been dismissed.
predicates.process_used_to_harass_or_pressure: The complainant used the criminal process to harass or pressure the accused in connection with the underlying dispute.
predicates.accused_liberty_restricted: The criminal process resulted in restrictions on the accused’s personal liberty or freedom of movement.

issues.definition: When a challenged criminal prosecution concerns a civil dispute already finally resolved, and repeated complaints, concealment of an earlier dismissal, use of process to pressure the accused, and restrictions on the accused’s liberty are present, the prosecution is quashed.
